title: Scientists Contest Dating of Van Gogh’s "The Starry Night"
description:
News
                The researchers identified discrepancies between the celestial alignments in June 1889 and Vincent van Gogh
body:
News
                The researchers identified discrepancies between the celestial alignments in June 1889 and Vincent van Gogh’s painted night sky.  
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Visitors taking a photo of Vincent Van Gogh's ''The Starry Night" (1889) at the Museum of Modern Art in New York City in November 2023 (photo Mairo Cinquetti/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
    
        
            Scholars have long accepted June 1889 as the month when Vincent van Gogh painted the iconic blue eddied-sky and idyllic hillside village of "The Starry Night." Yet a new Scientific Reports study published Thursday, October 22, calls for reconsidering that date, suggesting the Post-Impressionist painter may have drawn inspiration from a night sky that appeared a month later. South Korean researchers Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim, Suna Kang, Jungwoo Song, and Ho Jin argue that several celestial forms in the painting contradict the original June 1889 date and are better supported by the conditions of July that same year. The study incorporates tools that analyze star patterns and positions, contemporary weather models, van Gogh's letters, and other methods of inquiry in what the researchers call a "multidisciplinary framework." "Earlier astronomical readings, constrained by the conventional June dating, reached mutually exclusive conclusions, and the painting’s celestial arrangement was never quantitatively tested," the report's abstract reads. "These findings suggest that the night sky in The Starry Night originated from observation of a specific celestial arrangement, and call for reconsidering the June dating." In June 1889, the artist was weeks into his harrowing yearlong confinement at a French asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, a few months after he'd famously severed his left ear during a row with painter Paul Gauguin. The view from his asylum window was thought to have inspired his expressionist masterpiece, which is in the permanent collection of the Museum of Modern Art in Manhattan.

title: Kid Cudi to Write, Direct, and Star as Basquiat in New Biopic
description:
Film
                The rapper called his forthcoming film, "JEAN," a “love letter” to the late artist and ’80s New York in his
body:
Film
                The rapper called his forthcoming film, "JEAN," a “love letter” to the late artist and ’80s New York in his announcement on October 21.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Left: American artist Jean-Michel Basquiat (1960–88), c. 1985 (photo Rose Hartman via Getty Images); right: Kid Cudi in 2025 (photo Alan Chapman/Dave Benett via Getty Images)
    
        
            American rapper Kid Cudi took to Instagram this week to announce his hand in writing, directing, and starring in the forthcoming project JEAN, a biopic of late contemporary artist Jean-Michel Basquiat. Cudi called the film a “love letter to Jean, the 80s and NY city,” and said that production is set to begin next year.Cudi added that he will portray Basquiat, stating that the late artist has served as an inspiration to his career throughout, and that it'll be the “biggest honor to tell his story in a way we haven't seen before.”“This one im so proud of and excited about,” Cudi wrote in the caption accompanying the mockup promotional poster and several black-and-white photos of him as Basquiat in a large studio. “To write a film about someone who existed was a challenge, but it was a welcomed one. A lot of research, books, talks with people that knew him.”The announcement of JEAN comes after Cudi publicized his own foray into visual art in recent months. The multi-hyphenate artist debuted his painting practice under the name Scotty Ramon in a group presentation at Art Cologne 2025, and held his inaugural solo exhibition, Echoes of the Past, at the Paris location of Ruttkowski;68 this January. Scotty Ramon (Kid Cudi) shares one of his paintings, “WHEN THE LIGHT DIES,” on Instagram (screenshot Hyperallergic via Instagram)

title: Artists Take to the Streets Amid Massive Protests in France
description:
Art Week Paris
                Tens of thousands gathered at Porte d’Italie in Paris for a march led in part by culture-sector c
body:
Art Week Paris
                Tens of thousands gathered at Porte d’Italie in Paris for a march led in part by culture-sector coalitions demanding a better life for artists. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Artists, art students, and cultural workers joined hundreds of thousands of protesters marching across France on October 24, 2026. (photo Nicolas Tucat / AFP via Getty Images)
    
        
            PARIS — On the heels of last Saturday’s mass protests — and amid the preemptive closure of Art Basel Paris and museums like the Louvre — Paris’s artists, culture workers, and art students were back in the streets today, October 24. Tens of thousands gathered at Porte d’Italie for a march called in part by Cultures en Lutte, the network of culture-sector coalitions that has mobilized alongside the labor confederations and student unions since the movement began in mid-September, and by one of its driving forces, the National Union of Visual Artists (SNAP-CGT).  They came despite a week of warnings. After the destruction of October 17, the French government announced a “massive” security deployment: Sentinelle anti-terror soldiers would relieve police of guard duties, while special units would be backed by helicopters, armored vehicles, and water cannons. More than 250,000 protestors turned out anyway in Paris, and several hundred thousand more around the country, reports estimate. Police arrested approximately 1,000 protesters just today.  A painted sign depicts French President Emmanuel Macron using "our rights" as toilet paper.Students pose with their signs at the October 24 protest. The left sign warns against the use of AI; the right sign reads, “The boat is sinking, but the politicians are fighting over who will be captain.”

title: How Art Can Deliver Justice for Refugees
description:
Feature
                In the legal system, art created by refugees and incarcerated people can serve both as a form of therapy
body:
Feature
                In the legal system, art created by refugees and incarcerated people can serve both as a form of therapy and as evidence of mass atrocities.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            A woman weeps in the foreground of a painting by Rohingya artist Enayet Khan, set against scenes of violence committed by Myanmar’s military during the Rohingya genocide. (image courtesy Enayet Khan)
    
        
            Enayet Khan fled Myanmar in 2017. For three days, he moved through forests and fields with his family, slipping from one village to the next as fires closed in behind them. Each time they stopped, the safety was temporary — by morning, that village too would be burning. His own home had already been reduced to ash, but there was no time to mourn what was lost. Armed soldiers moved quickly, and Khan saw people being shot in front of him. The goal was simple : to survive long enough to find a way out of Myanmar. Ten members of his family fled together; three were injured along the way. Eventually, they crossed the border into Bangladesh.“I lost everything,” Khan told Hyperallergic in a phone call. “Home, documentation, property, a sense of security.”Khan settled in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, now home to nearly one million Rohingya refugees. The Rohingya people have endured decades of discrimination and repression under Myanmar’s successive governments. Stripped of citizenship by a 1982 law, they remain one of the largest stateless groups in the world. Most fled in 2017 to escape the military’s crimes against humanity and genocide.In the camps, Khan turned to painting and drawing to process the atrocities he had witnessed: burning homes, fleeing families, and executions. Over time, he began training other refugees to do the same, establishing the Rohingya Art Club (RAC) and encouraging visual storytelling as a form of expression and resistance.Khan is one of many refugees using art to record experiences of conflict and violence. According to legal experts, such work can also play a role in accountability efforts, helping to convey testimony and corroborate survivor accounts, and even enter legal proceedings as evidence of mass atrocities.A record 117.8 million people have been forcibly displaced worldwide — a number that has risen for 12 consecutive years. Investigations and prosecutions of genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes have surged within the European Union, with new cases increasing by 44% between 2016 and 2021. Today, more displaced people are turning to international courts to hold perpetrators accountable, an increase in demand that the International Criminal Court (ICC) itself has called “unprecedented.”For some legal advocates, art has become one way to meet that demand. Khan’s painting depicting scenes he witnessed during the Rohingya genocide, including burning homes, fleeing families, and summary executions carried out by Myanmar’s military (image courtesy Enayet Khan)Antonia Mulvey, executive director of Legal Action Worldwide and a former United Nations investigator, collected artwork as part of the evidence in a case before the International Court of Justice that charged the Myanmar military with genocide against Rohingya communities in 2017. She noted that the high illiteracy rate among Rohingya people, especially women and children, makes it difficult to record traditional statements. In those contexts, drawings became a vital way to convey their testimonies.

title: The War on Art Is Repeating Itself
description:
Book Review
                As an artist who lived through the Reagan-era Culture Wars, I recommend Isaac Butler’s “The Perfect
body:
Book Review
                As an artist who lived through the Reagan-era Culture Wars, I recommend Isaac Butler’s “The Perfect Moment” for the stories that parallel our current fight to defend creative expression.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            A self-portrait by Robert Mapplethorpe projected onto the facade of the Corcoran Gallery of Art during a protest on 30, 1989 (photo Carol Guzy/the Washington Post via Getty Images, all images courtesy Bloomsbury)
    
        
            Critic and theater director Isaac Butler is younger than I am, so he didn’t live through the Culture Wars of the Reagan ’80s. During this time, for instance, the Morality Action Committee wrote postcards to legislators across the country claiming that Franklin Furnace — the arts organization I founded 50 years ago — had shown pornography to 500 children per day during our Carnival Knowledge exhibition of women artists exploring sexuality. But as an art aficionado, he saw an alarming development in 2020, when an exhibition of Philip Guston’s work was postponed by the Tate Modern; the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston; the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston; and the National Gallery of Art for fear that his paintings referencing the Ku Klux Klan might be misinterpreted by the public. In light of the current rise of right-wing legislators, politicians, and organizations targeting arts and culture in the United States, the parallel story of the conservative players of the 1980s and ’90s needs to be told. Butler’s book, The Perfect Moment: God, Sex, Art, and the Birth of America's Culture Wars (2026), discusses major events in that tumultuous era of the 1980s and ’90s, including the difficulty Martin Scorsese had producing The Last Temptation of Christ (1988), primarily caused by Reverend Donald Wildmon’s innovation of mass mailing to Christians on behalf of his National Federation for Decency. Wildmon appears again in Butler’s discussion of Andres Serrano’s infamous “Piss Christ” (1987), a photograph of a plastic crucifix in a beaker of the artist’s urine. In 1989, then-Senator Alfonse D’Amato ripped a reproduction of a catalog image of Serrano’s artwork in half on the Senate floor.Cover of The Perfect Moment: God, Sex, Art, and the Birth of America's Culture Wars by Isaac Butler (Bloomsbury, 2026)Then there’s the story that gives the book its name: the cancellation of The Perfect Moment, a Robert Mapplethorpe retrospective, by the Corcoran Gallery of Art in Washington, DC. By the mid-1980s, Mapplethorpe’s AIDS diagnosis had become common knowledge. Although The Perfect Moment had traveled nationally, its depiction of sadomasochism, Black nude models, and naked children was likely going to get a reaction in Washington. So on June 12, 1989, the Corcoran Gallery of Art decided to cancel the exhibition before it opened, after which Jesse Helms and Sidney Yates, a Democratic Congressman from Illinois, fought over the funding of the National Endowment for the Arts (NEA) itself. Butler provides a balanced account of how both sides strategized and implemented their ambitions.

title: The Center Cannot Hold at the Toronto Biennial
description:
Art Review
                It’s a provocative and discursive exploration of how artists respond to our late-capitalist epoch, bu
body:
Art Review
                It’s a provocative and discursive exploration of how artists respond to our late-capitalist epoch, but its focus on “rupture” raises questions.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Detail of Wen Liu, "In Light, Where Edges Yield" (2025), prescribed herbal medicine, epoxy clay, resin, acrylic, varnish, stainless steel (photo Rebecca Tisdelle-Macias, courtesy Toronto Biennial of Art; all other photos Neil Price/Hyperallergic)
    
        
            TORONTO — At the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, this year, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney declared that the world is “in the midst of a rupture, not a transition.” The line is quoted in the catalog for the fourth Toronto Biennial of Art, Things Fall Apart, and could serve as the exhibition’s epigraph. Curated by Allison Glenn, who spent her childhood in Detroit, crossing into Canada through Windsor, the edition brings together more than 30 artists and collectives across Toronto and, for the first time, sites beyond it, including Anchorage in Alaska and Times Square in New York.Glenn keeps the Biennial’s long-running focus on water, taking the Great Lakes as her point of departure to ask what artists who work with rupture can teach us about histories, borders, and movement. With Canada–United States relations at an unprecedented low, a cross-border exhibition built around shared waterways feels just right.Installation view of works by Dawoud BeyThe most affecting works treat histories of rupture as an imaginative encounter to be conjured rather than a settled narrative to be recorded. At the Art Gallery of Ontario (AGO), Dawoud Bey’s Material Histories, Living Landscapes hangs photographs from three landscape series tightly together around his two-channel video “350,000” (2023), alongside sculptures and ritual objects from the AGO’s collection with roots in Nigeria, Ghana, and the Kingdom of Kongo. The pairing sets up a striking sonic and visual call and response across the Middle Passage, elucidating the ways the afterlife of slavery permeates the physical world around us. The film’s point-of-view movement through dense woods, accompanied by the sound of heavy breathing and black-and-white images of gnarled landscapes and old homes, suggests that the fight to live free from racial violence is still an urgent one today.  At the University of Toronto Art Centre, the exhibition’s main venue, Antonio Obá strings rows of brass bells across the length of a gallery for “Jardim” (2022–26), which visitors brush against as they walk a processional path. The work sounds only when bodies move through it; memory here is repeatedly reperformed rather than stored as an unchanging artifact. The path leads to “A Folia: travessia” (The Revelry: A Crossing, 2026), a large painting that reimagines Douglas Martin’s 1957 photograph of 15-year-old Dorothy Counts integrating a high school in Charlotte, North Carolina. Obá replaces the crowd that jeered and spat at her with one resembling both a supportive march and a New Orleans-style street carnival, a striking intervention within a painful chapter in history that points us toward a restorative alternate reality. He's asking us to imagine being there with Dorothy in that moment, surrounding her with courage and love; to let go of fear and hatred; to march toward and for a better future.Installation view of Wen Liu, "In Light, Where Edges Yield" (2025), prescribed herbal medicine, epoxy clay, resin, acrylic, varnish, stainless steelMoving from the historical to the personal, a second group of works takes knowledge held in bodies, materials, and practice as its guide. Wen Liu’s “In Light, Where Edges Yield” (2025), a human-scale steel-and-resin sculpture built around a spinal column, suspends Chinese herbal medicines prescribed to the artist after her father’s death, the herbs glowing like stained glass. It suggests that the body acts as an important source of familial and personal knowledge that might both illuminate our experience and carry us through difficult, disruptive periods.  Taqralik Partridge’s “umiakkut (by boat)” (2026) revisits the journey her grandmother and siblings made across the Hudson Strait in a umiaq boat used by Indigenous Arctic peoples. In a mirrored room, she conjures the vessel, usually made with animal skins, from found materials, sewing, and beadwork, while an elder relative’s voice drifts through a soundtrack of water, passing on intergenerational knowledge that serves as a guide in this time of ecological devastation. Installation views of Taqralik Partridge, "Tuktujuq" (2024), reindeer hide and skull, glass beads, dental floss, red fox, Celine Dion CDs, vinyl floor, soundtrack, four wall videosTwo standout works use place to reunite what was once separated. At the Royal Ontario Museum, Raphaël Barontini fills the Crystal Court with massive, draped textile panels that fold images of masks and sacred objects from the museum’s collections into an allegory of the Americas. “Follow the North Star – a Tribute to Harriet Tubman” (2026) connects Caribbean aesthetics that include anti-slavery heroines, water gods, and mythical figures to the Underground Railroad, a secret network that guided Black freedom seekers out of American slavery to a Canadian freedom still marred by racism. It casts liberation as a collective struggle that transcends not only geographic borders but the divide between the physical and spiritual. Meanwhile, in the nearby town of Scarborough, Nirbhai (nep) Singh Sidhu’s “A Deathless Potential In Remembrance By You” (2026), a permanent structure at the Scarborough Gurdwara built with earth from Sirhind, Punjab, is made for simran, the Sikh practice of stillness and deep listening. Bricks, steel, and water come together, binding paths of spiritual awakening to survival.Raphaël Barontini, "Follow the North Star – a Tribute to Harriet Tubman" (2026)A final highlight, Rouzbeh Akhbari’s “Of Wool and Diesel” (2026) at Mercer Union, moves from these embodied and spiritual paths to geopolitical and economic ones. The 30-minute film follows the informal sheep trade around the Strait of Hormuz, binding shepherds and flocks to smugglers and moneychangers. Made as war in Iran was shutting down trade routes, it refuses to treat rupture as enclosure. Borders close, routes collapse, yet people and exchange persist.Spread across more than 13 Toronto sites, with plenty of programming still to come, Things Fall Apart is ambitious and timely. It's a provocative and discursive exploration of how artists respond to our late-capitalist epoch with works that adapt to its social, political, and ecological realities rather than mourn what has broken. One challenge, though, is cohesion. The physical distance between sites and the dizzying range of subjects, from Inuit migration to Gulf smuggling, make it hard to hold as a whole.Nirbhai (nep) Singh Sidhu, "A Deathless Potential In Remembrance By You" (2026), simran, clay, sand, concrete, steel, rock;But the deeper problem lies in the exhibition’s foundational concept. Rupture, as Carney and others envision it, presupposes a prior unity, and the exhibition never satisfactorily examines or troubles that perceived unity. Glenn’s catalog essay raises the right question (rupture to what, and by whom?), but the exhibition seldom pursues it with rigor. As I encountered each work, I repeatedly felt myself asking: Was there a time since modernity — which is inextricably tied to slavery, colonial extraction, empire, forced migration, genocide — when the so-called world order did not feel ruinous to those on its underside? The rupture may be less new than newly felt by those who have sought to order the world to their liking.Things Fall Apart, the fourth iteration of the Toronto Biennial of Art, continues at venues across Toronto as well as select sites elsewhere through December 20. The exhibition was curated by Allison Glenn.

title: This Is Class War
description:
Weekly Newsletter
                The latest on the student protests in France, the art world’s AI problem, one-on-one with Rosa
body:
Weekly Newsletter
                The latest on the student protests in France, the art world’s AI problem, one-on-one with Rosana Paulino, and Beer With a Painter featuring Melissa Brown.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
    
        
            The subway car rattles, shakes, and screeches as it tunnels us from Brooklyn to Manhattan underneath the East River. I hold on tight to a pole, while my eyes are fixed on an ad for the Broadway musical Les Misérables. My social media feed shows me only looting and vandalism in France, painting a violent picture of the largely peaceful student protests. Panicking, the art world’s blue-chip class shuts down Art Basel Paris early and flees the city. The Louvre also closes to protect its treasures. Loot a little and they throw you in jail; loot a lot and they let you open a museum. I get to a benefit dinner for an art residency held in a former bank. A peppy auctioneer asks the who’s who to open their hearts and wallets. Paddles go up and down, and a donation ticker on a big screen climbs to astronomical numbers while I admire the building’s huge stained-glass skylight. Up there, near a golden clock that no longer ticks, an inscription in marble letters reads, "It's what we save rather than what we earn that ensures a competence for the future."Outside, Midtown Manhattan is huffing and puffing, and the neon lights glow too bright. A sign in a bodega window advertises that the Powerball jackpot has hit $650 million, and I drift into a daydream about what my life would be like if I won that much money. I picture myself raising the paddle at auctions and amassing a serious art collection — just to support artists, you know. I sit somewhere for a coffee and see the barista trying to buy a ticket on her phone for a new movie about white-collar convicted criminal Elizabeth Holmes, who’s become a cultural icon among the petite bourgeoisie. The barista can’t find a ticket because the theater is sold out.  On the subway ride back home, I get sucked into an essay about Kazimir Malevich’s concept of the “White Abyss” and miss my stop by several stations, adding an hour to my commute. I get off in an impoverished neighborhood and see that someone has graffitied “Class War” all over a residential building. There’s nothing open but a convenience store at a gas station. Fuck it, I’m buying a Powerball ticket.—Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief

	
		
			Dear Art World, We Can Tell When You’re Using AI
		
	
	
		Wall labels. Press releases. Artist statements. In today’s fast-paced art world, the written word stands at a crucial crossroads — and the stakes have never been higher. But here’s the thing: It’s not just about convenience. It’s about authenticity. Because the way we express ourselves matters.

The above paragraph was generated by Claude when prompted to write an introduction for an opinion piece against AI use in art writing, and if it made you recoil in your seat, you may be among those of us who have developed a strong aversion to generative text. You’ll know it when you see it: that uncanny cadence that’s overconfident in style yet hollow in substance, like a motivational LinkedIn post that feels relatable at first but leaves you with as much nourishment as a spoonful of Stevia. | Valentina Di Liscia
